title: Rejoicing
hook: a friend posts the win you wanted; Shantideva opens chapter three by being glad for everyone
tomorrow: he wishes he were something you swallow. what is it?

segments.voice: Chapter two closed on confession: a wrong said out loud, to beings who already knew, so it could be mended. Said out loud. Chapter three opens on the other side of the ledger: other people's good.
screen: `SAID OUT LOUD.` → `CHAPTER THREE: OTHER PEOPLE'S GOOD.`

segments.voice: The group chat lights up. A friend got the thing you both applied for: the spot, the part, the prize. There's a photo. Everyone's sending hearts. Your thumb hovers over the keyboard, and what comes up first isn't joy. It's a small, hot question: why her? So, yesterday's question, asked straight: can you be glad for someone who just beat you? Shantideva starts chapter three by trying, on purpose, with everyone. And inside Buddhism there's more than one view of how honest that is.
screen: `THE GROUP CHAT LIGHTS UP.` → `WHY HER?` → `GLAD FOR SOMEONE WHO BEAT YOU?`

segments.voice: First voice: Shantideva. Chapter three opens with him rejoicing, gladly, in the good done by all beings, the good that eases their suffering. He rejoices in those set free, in the bodhisattvas' long road, in the Buddhas' awakening. The word is anumodana, rejoicing in someone else's good. His best case: rejoicing is a practice, not a mood. You do it before you feel it, the way you stretch before you're flexible, and envy loosens. And it judges the deed, not the doer: a hungry person who got fed is fed, whoever posted the photo. Second voice, which leans on the Buddha's own words in the Pali suttas: intention, he says, is what makes an act what it is. So a good deed done to be seen is mixed. Its best case: honest people shouldn't cheer vanity as if it were pure, and saying congratulations you don't feel can turn into a habit of saying things you don't mean. Where they meet: Shantideva never claims motives don't matter, and the second voice never says don't be glad. One says start with the gladness. The other says keep it honest. Glad for all.
screen: `SHANTIDEVA: REJOICE IN ALL GOOD.` · `A PRACTICE, NOT A MOOD.` · `THE OTHER VOICE: INTENTION IS THE ACT.` · `START GLAD, AND KEEP IT HONEST.` · then, large: `GLAD FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Count three good things other people did recently, one on each finger: a kindness you saw, something a friend pulled off, a stranger who held a door. Pause on each one and let yourself be glad it happened, even if you had no part in it.
Rejoicing: being glad for the good someone else did. Shantideva treats it as a practice you start before the feeling arrives.
The line for today: glad for all, starting with the one who beat you. Chapter three, begun.

howItsDone: In Theravada temples, people answer a good deed or a shared blessing with sadhu, sadhu, sadhu, an expression of rejoicing; in Mahayana practice, rejoicing in others' good is one of the regular steps of a daily liturgy.

fork.setup: a classmate posts photos of herself volunteering, clearly for the likes. a friend says rejoicing in it would be fake. what's the fairest version of your friend's view?
options: intention shapes the act, so cheering a show as pure would be dishonest.
volunteering for likes does no good at all, so there's nothing to rejoice in.
rejoicing is for monks; ordinary people should just mind their own business.
fork.reveal: that's the second voice at its best. Shantideva's reply: the people she helped were still helped, so rejoice in that good, without praising the show.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: rejoicing in, approving of someone else's good. Chapter three opens with it.

trapdoor: what you thought: rejoicing is just being happy when good things happen to you.
what it means: it's being glad for other people's good, everyone's, including the one who beat you.

what a scholar hears: anumodana, a practice shared by the Theravada (sadhu) and the Mahayana; Shantideva's version reaches from ordinary kindness to the Buddhas' awakening, while the suttas' teaching on intention keeps it honest.
guess: being glad for the good someone else has done
a festival held when the temple's harvest comes in
celebrating loudly so that others can see your joy

chat.says: ava won the regional art prize. mine didn't place. i said congrats but it felt fake. is that bad?
options: Not bad. Rejoicing is practice: be glad for her good now; the feeling can catch up.
Kind of. If you don't feel it, saying congrats is a lie, so say nothing.
It's fine. Congrats is just manners; nobody actually means it anyway.
chat.meaning: Shantideva rejoices on purpose, before the feeling arrives; the other voice keeps it honest. Being glad for Ava's good is real, envy and all.

notes: Debate shape: two voices inside Buddhism, Shantideva's practice of rejoicing (3.1-3.4) and the suttas' teaching that intention is kamma (AN 6.63), both given their best case; no school is labeled or ranked. The 'second voice' is a reasonable application of AN 6.63, not a named school's position on rejoicing; confirm the framing is fair.
'A practice, not a mood... you do it before you feel it' interprets Shantideva's deliberate rejoicing; confirm.
